entries.statement: Trust zones (logical network "Spaces") are enforced; cross-zone traffic flows only via governed integration layers (gateway/bus).
entries.justification: The app has four clearly separated zones: the browser (not trusted), the app itself (trusted; listens only on this computer unless told otherwise), the data (trusted; database and files protected by file permissions) and outside providers (reached only through an allow-list of permitted addresses). Everything that crosses a zone boundary goes through the app's own checks.
entries.deploymentNote: The same zones apply once the app is online, but the app must then sit behind a TLS (HTTPS) proxy so the browser-to-app boundary is encrypted (see AC-01).
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: yes.
entries.note: Your app is built in separate compartments, so a problem in one part (for example a bad request from a browser) cannot reach your data directly.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Service addressing & discovery are unified and consistent across environments; intra-zone shortcuts are not used externally.
entries.justification: The app is a single program with one address. There are no other services that need to find or address each other.
entries.note: This control is for systems made of many services. Your app is one program, so there is nothing to do.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Service boundaries are clear; no circular dependencies; services are right-sized; each service owns its data.
entries.justification: One program owns its one database. Each feature (accounts, admin, uploads, the assistant, your own records) is a separate module that talks to the database through the same shared helpers, with no circular dependencies between modules.
entries.note: Your app is organised so that each feature is self-contained and easy to check.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Architecture avoids long synchronous chains; event-driven or queued handoffs are used where appropriate.
entries.justification: There are no chains of services calling each other; every request is handled by the single app, with short timeouts on any outbound call.
entries.note: This control is about long chains of services waiting on each other. Your app has none.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: API/event contracts are defined and versioned; consumers are notified before breaking changes take effect.
entries.justification: Every route is declared in a central registry with its input rules, and a machine-readable description of the API (docs/openapi.json and docs/api.md) is generated from it. Changes to the API are visible in that file.
entries.note: Your app comes with an up-to-date description of every page and API route it offers.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Messaging has durability (persistence/replication/retention) with a defined DLQ strategy and triage.
entries.justification: The app does not use a message queue or event bus, so there is no messaging durability to design.
entries.note: This control is for systems that pass messages between services. Your app does not.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Startup resilience: services handle missing dependencies; autoscaling defined with minimum replicas.
entries.justification: The app checks all of its settings when it starts and refuses to start with a clear message if anything is missing or unsafe, instead of running half-working. Automatic scaling does not apply to an app that runs on one computer (that part of the control is not applicable).
entries.deploymentNote: If the app is later hosted online, ask the hosting provider about running more than one copy and restarting it automatically.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: deferred.
entries.note: If a setting is wrong, the app tells you at start-up instead of failing later in a confusing way.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Legacy integrations are isolated behind an anti-corruption layer; migration path is defined.
entries.justification: The app is new and does not connect to any older (legacy) system.
entries.note: This control is about connecting to old systems. Your app does not.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Data are classified with named owners; controls are proportional to classification.
entries.justification: The app stores only business or internal data, no information about people. docs/data-protection.md records this classification and names you as the owner.
entries.note: Your app stores no personal information, and the report says so in writing.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Encryption in transit (TLS/mTLS) and at rest with managed keys and rotation is designed in.
entries.justification: The app runs on this computer only, so traffic never crosses a network, and it stores no personal or sensitive information that would need encrypting at rest. Database files are protected by file permissions.
entries.deploymentNote: If the app is ever reached over a network it must run behind a TLS (HTTPS) proxy; see docs/deployment.md.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: no.
entries.note: Your app stays on this computer and stores nothing sensitive, so encryption is not needed yet.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Handlers and workflows are idempotent; duplicate detection/suppression is in place where needed.
entries.justification: API requests that change data honour an Idempotency-Key header (a repeated request returns the stored answer instead of acting twice), and the database has unique constraints that prevent duplicate records.
entries.note: If a request is accidentally sent twice (for example after a network hiccup), the app does not create two records.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Cross-service transactions use Sagas/compensations; 2PC is avoided; prefer intra-service ACID first.
entries.justification: There is a single database, and multi-step changes run inside one database transaction that either fully succeeds or is rolled back. No cross-service transactions exist.
entries.note: This control is for changes spread across several services. Your app uses one database with all-or-nothing updates.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Retention/deletion policies exist per data class; minimization is applied to collection/storage.
entries.justification: The app stores only the business data you defined and no information about people. docs/data-retention.md records what is kept and that nothing needs a deletion schedule.
entries.note: Your app keeps only the information you asked for.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Consistency model is documented; UX handles staleness/conflicts; event-sourcing considered where appropriate.
entries.justification: There is one database and every read sees the latest write, so there is no staleness or conflict handling to design. Records carry an updated_at value that prevents two people silently overwriting each other's edit.
entries.note: This control is for systems where data can be out of date in different places. Your app has one source of truth.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Retries use exponential backoff + jitter; default exception handling and safe error models exist.
entries.justification: Errors are handled centrally: people see a short, generic message and the details go to the log, never to the browser. Outbound calls to other services retry a limited number of times with increasing, randomised delays.
entries.note: When something goes wrong, your app fails safely and does not reveal internal details.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Circuit breakers/bulkheads protect dependencies; non-critical features have fallback/degraded modes.
entries.justification: Calls to other services go through one outbound client with a circuit breaker: after repeated failures the app stops calling the service for a while and shows a friendly 'temporarily unavailable' message instead of hanging.
entries.note: If a service your app depends on is down, your app keeps working for everything else.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Asynchronous semantics are defined: ordering, delivery guarantees, ack/visibility timeouts; DLQs are monitored.
entries.justification: The app has no background jobs or message queues, so there are no asynchronous semantics to define.
entries.note: This control is for background processing. Your app does everything while you wait.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Shared integration layers (gateway/bus) are high-availability and contain errors to prevent cross-zone failure propagation.
entries.justification: There is no shared gateway or message bus between services; the app is a single program.
entries.note: This control is for shared infrastructure between many services. Your app has none.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: All mutating endpoints enforce an Idempotency-Key; concurrency controls (locks/optimistic concurrency) are in place.
entries.justification: API requests that change data honour an Idempotency-Key header, and edits check the record's updated_at value so two people cannot silently overwrite each other's change.
entries.note: Repeated or overlapping edits are handled safely.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Timeouts on all calls; health probes; explicit failover/multi-AZ strategies for critical paths.
entries.justification: Every incoming request and every outbound call has a timeout, and the app offers /healthz and /readyz endpoints so it can be checked automatically. Failover to a second location is not applicable to an app on one computer.
entries.deploymentNote: When hosting online, ask the provider to monitor /healthz and to run the app in more than one place if downtime would be costly.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: deferred.
entries.note: Your app never waits forever on anything, and it can tell a monitoring tool whether it is healthy.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Quotas and autoscaling are defined; rate-limits enforced at edges; minimum capacity documented.
entries.justification: Rate limits are enforced by the app itself on sign-in, registration, password reset, the assistant, uploads and all other routes, and each person has quotas for the records and files they create. Automatic scaling does not apply to an app on one computer.
entries.deploymentNote: When hosting online, keep the app's limits and add the provider's own protection against floods of traffic if available.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: yes.
entries.note: Nobody can flood your app with requests or fill it with unlimited data.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Caching/CDN/back-pressure patterns are applied where appropriate; performance guardrails are defined.
entries.justification: There is no caching layer or content delivery network. Basic performance guardrails are still in place: request size limits, timeouts and a maximum number of rows per list.
entries.note: This control is for large systems with caches. Your app has simple built-in limits instead.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: All communications use TLS/mTLS; service identity is verified (e.g., mesh-issued certs).
entries.justification: The app listens only on this computer's loopback address, so its traffic never travels over a network and there is no connection to encrypt. Service identity checks between services do not apply to a single program.

actions.text: If you ever want to reach the app from another computer, first run it in a TLS mode (behind an HTTPS proxy or with a certificate) as described in docs/deployment.md.

entries.deploymentNote: Becomes 'no' the moment the app is reached over a network without TLS; run it behind an HTTPS proxy first.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: no.
entries.note: While the app stays on this computer, nothing travels over a network that could be intercepted.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Central IdP (OIDC/OAuth2) is used; MFA enforced on privileged/admin paths; tokens are short-lived.
entries.justification: The app keeps its own accounts instead of using a central sign-in system (identity provider). The most important parts of this control are still in place: administrators must use two-factor authentication with an authenticator app, sessions expire after inactivity and after a fixed time, and every user may turn on two-factor authentication.

actions.text: If your organisation has a central sign-in system (for example Microsoft Entra, Google Workspace or Okta), have a developer connect the app to it with OpenID Connect before it is used across several teams.

entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: no.
entries.note: Your app has its own accounts with strong protection for administrators. Connecting it to a company-wide sign-in system is a later improvement, not a requirement to start using it.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: RBAC/ABAC governs APIs and publish/consume on messaging; least privilege is applied.
entries.justification: Every route declares who may use it (public, any signed-in person, or specific roles) in the central registry; anything not declared is refused. Records that belong to a person can only be opened by that person or an administrator. Each role gets only the access it needs.
entries.note: People can only see and do what their role allows, and this is checked on every request.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Authorization is centralized at gateway/mesh via policy-as-code; shared integration services are governed.
entries.justification: There is no API gateway or service mesh; the app is a single program. As a compensating control, authorisation is centralised in the app's route registry rather than scattered across the code.
entries.note: This control is for systems with many services behind a gateway. Your app centralises access rules in one place instead.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Secrets are stored in a secret manager; keys/certs rotate automatically; no secrets in code/logs.
entries.justification: Secrets (session key, encryption keys, API keys) are generated strong by SecureVibe, kept in a .env file with strict file permissions, never written into code or logs, and the app refuses to start with weak or placeholder values. However there is no dedicated secret manager and keys do not rotate automatically; the field-encryption key can be rotated with a command.

actions.text: When the app is hosted online, move its secrets from the .env file into the hosting provider's secret manager and set up regular key rotation.

entries.deploymentNote: Becomes 'yes' once secrets live in a secret manager with automatic rotation.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: no.
entries.note: Your app's secret keys are strong and stored safely on this computer. A secret manager is a hosting feature to add when the app goes online.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Applicable regulatory controls (e.g., privacy/financial) are identified with evidence of design alignment.
entries.justification: The app handles no personal, financial or health information, so no specific privacy or financial regulation has been identified as applying to it.
entries.note: No special regulations were identified for the kind of information your app stores.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Least privilege extends to CI/CD, VCS apps, chat-ops, and third-party tooling; periodic reviews are scheduled.
entries.justification: There is no CI/CD pipeline, source-hosting app or chat-ops tooling connected to the app; it is built and run on this computer.
entries.note: If you later add automation tools (for example an online code repository with automatic builds), give each tool only the access it needs and review that access regularly.
entries.verificationNote: Not applicable by design; nothing to contradict it.

entries.statement: Structured centralized logs with correlation/trace IDs; administrative access is logged.
entries.justification: The app writes structured (JSON) logs with a request id on every line, so one request can be followed end to end. Sign-ins, denied access, administrator actions and unexpected errors are all recorded. Centralised log collection does not apply on a single computer.
entries.deploymentNote: When hosting online, send the logs to a central log service so they survive if the server is compromised.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: deferred.
entries.note: Your app keeps a clear record of what happened and who did it.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: Metrics/SLOs and dashboards cover service health and event-flow anomalies; alerts are actionable.
entries.justification: The app exposes health endpoints and logs, but there are no dashboards, service-level objectives or alerts. On a single computer this is acceptable; it becomes important once the app is hosted for others.

actions.text: When the app is hosted online, add uptime monitoring on /healthz and an alert for repeated errors or failed sign-ins.

entries.deploymentNote: Becomes 'yes' once monitoring and alerts are in place at the hosting provider.
entries.comment: Status once deployed on the internet: no.
entries.note: Nothing watches your app automatically yet. That is fine on your own computer; add monitoring when it goes online.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: ASVS-aligned security tests and negative tests from threat-modeling are planned in the test strategy.
entries.justification: The app ships with a security test suite whose tests are named after the OWASP ASVS requirements they check, plus negative tests (things that must be refused) derived from the threat model, such as anonymous access, wrong role, bad input and ownership violations.
entries.note: Your app comes with automatic tests that prove its protections work, and you can run them again any time.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: SbD controls are verifiable in test (isolation, mTLS, authZ denials, rate-limit behavior).
entries.justification: The design controls can be checked automatically: the tests and the runtime scan verify denied access for anonymous and wrong-role users, ownership checks, CSRF protection, rate limits and security headers on the running app.
entries.note: The protections in the design are not just on paper: SecureVibe tests them on the running app.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

entries.statement: OpenAPI/AsyncAPI and event catalogs are published; ADRs/runbooks are current.
entries.justification: A machine-readable API description (docs/openapi.json), the design decisions (docs/adr) and the operating documents (SECURITY.md, deployment, incident response, data retention) are generated from the design and the code, so they stay current.
entries.note: Your app's documentation is generated from the real code, so it does not go stale.
entries.verificationNote: This was decided at design time; the build produced no independent check of it.

sbd.summary: Because it includes an AI assistant that accepts untrusted input, SecureVibe gets extra care. What we did: we wrote a threat model that lists 22 ways things could go wrong and the protection for each. 1 of them needs an action from you before the app is used for real. It is listed in the threat model. Some protections that big companies use (AC-02 and MT-06) do not exist for an app on one computer. Each has a plan with a date and an owner. Please read the threat model and confirm you understand it. No outside security expert reviewed it. After the build, 14 of 36 checklist items were confirmed by what was actually built.

summary.targetLevelRule: Level 2 (standard) because it includes an AI assistant that accepts untrusted input.

results.description: Verify that input is decoded or unescaped into a canonical form only once, it is only decoded when encoded data in that form is expected, and that this is done before processing the input further, for example it is not performed after input validation or sanitization.
results.rationale: Abby confirmed this manually on 2026-09-17. It is recorded, not independently verified.
results.plainLanguage: When the app unpacks encoded text (for example web addresses written with %20 codes), it does so once, only where such encoding is expected, and before it checks the text. Checking first and unpacking later would let a disguised value slip past the check.

steps: Search the code for decodeURIComponent, Buffer.from(..., 'base64') and similar decoding calls.
Confirm each decode happens before any validation of the same value, and that the value is not decoded a second time later.
manualVerification.whatCountsAsEvidence: A short list of every decode call and the line where the value is validated afterwards.

results.description: Verify that the application performs output encoding and escaping either as a final step before being used by the interpreter for which it is intended or by the interpreter itself.
results.rationale: Abby confirmed this manually on 2026-09-17. It is recorded, not independently verified.
results.plainLanguage: Text is made safe for a web page at the very last moment, when it is put into the page, or by the page engine itself. Doing it earlier risks the protection being undone.

steps: Open the page templates (src/views) and confirm data is inserted with <%= %>, which escapes automatically.
Confirm no code pre-escapes values and then inserts them with <%- %>.
manualVerification.whatCountsAsEvidence: Template files use <%= %> for all user-provided data; no manual escaping helpers are used before rendering.

results.description: Verify that output encoding for an HTTP response, HTML document, or XML document is relevant for the context required, such as encoding the relevant characters for HTML elements, HTML attributes, HTML comments, CSS, or HTTP header fields, to avoid changing the message or document structure.

evidence.summary: Runtime probe "dast.xss.reflected-smoke" passed: no unescaped reflection in the form, query or 404 responses.
No issues were detected by the static analysis rules that cover this requirement.

results.rationale: Verified by 1 runtime probe and 1 scanner check.
results.plainLanguage: Anything a user typed is made safe before it is shown on a page, so it cannot turn into hidden code that runs in other people's browsers.

steps: Sign in and enter the text test into any text field that is shown back later.
Open the page that displays it. The text must appear literally, with no bold formatting and no pop-up.
manualVerification.whatCountsAsEvidence: A screenshot showing the typed text displayed exactly as typed.

results.description: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
results.rationale: 2 open findings (F-0147, F-0149) contradict this requirement.
results.remediation: F-0147: Only allow http and https links; otherwise render plain text. F-0149: Only allow http and https links; otherwise render plain text.
results.plainLanguage: When the app builds a web address from something a user typed, it encodes the text and only allows normal web links (http or https), never links that would run code.

steps: Search the code for places that build a URL or href from user data.
Confirm the value is passed through encodeURIComponent and that the scheme is checked to be http or https.
manualVerification.whatCountsAsEvidence: A list of URL-building code locations showing encoding and a scheme check.

results.description: Verify that output encoding or escaping is used when dynamically building JavaScript content (including JSON), to avoid changing the message or document structure (to avoid JavaScript and JSON injection).

evidence.summary: No issues were detected by the static analysis rules that cover this requirement.

results.rationale: A single static check passed (1 scanner check); one more independent check, a test or a runtime probe would be needed to verify it.
results.remediation: Search templates and scripts for user data placed inside <script> blocks or built into JSON by string joining. Confirm JSON is produced with JSON.stringify or res.json, and that nothing user-provided is written directly inside a script tag.
results.plainLanguage: When user text is placed inside JavaScript or JSON that the browser will run, it is encoded so it cannot break out and become code.

steps: Search templates and scripts for user data placed inside <script> blocks or built into JSON by string joining.
Confirm JSON is produced with JSON.stringify or res.json, and that nothing user-provided is written directly inside a script tag.
manualVerification.whatCountsAsEvidence: No template inserts user data inside script tags; API responses are built with res.json.

results.description: Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures.

traceability.statement: SecureVibe only listens on this computer. Nothing on the network can reach it.
Every piece of input is checked on the server before it is used. Unexpected fields are rejected.
The browser is protected: strict security headers, no cross-site request forgery, no inline scripts.
When something goes wrong, people see a short generic message. Technical details never leak.
Security-relevant actions (sign-ins, denied access, changes by administrators) are recorded in a tamper-evident log kept for at least 12 months.
The app limits how many requests one person or address can make, stops slow requests, and reports whether it is healthy.
Secrets and keys live only in the configuration file, never in code, logs or reports.
Third-party packages are locked to tested versions, inventoried, and checked for known problems.
A written incident plan names The person running SecureVibe on this computer as the security contact and says what to do when something goes wrong.
Saving the same form twice, or two people editing at once, never corrupts a record.
People must sign in with a password of at least 12 characters before using SecureVibe. Guessing attempts are slowed down and locked temporarily.
Each role only gets what it needs (Administrator). Records with an owner are visible only to that owner and administrators.
Sessions end after 15 minutes of inactivity and after 8 hours at most. Logging out works on every page and ends the session on the server.
No account exists with a default password. The first administrator gets a one-time password that must be changed.
Every person may turn on an authenticator app for their own account.
Changing an email address or the authenticator setting requires the password again.
The AI assistant treats everything typed into it as untrusted, screens it for trickery, and checks every answer before showing it.
The assistant only sees the signed-in person's own records, always through the signed-in person's own permissions.
Every AI request is logged with its cost. Each person has a daily budget, and an administrator can switch the assistant off at once.
The assistant can propose a change, but nothing happens until the person confirms it.
SecureVibe only talks to the outside services named in its configuration. Each call has a time limit and a failure never takes the app down.

methodology: SecureVibe checked this application with automated tests, runtime probes against the running app, static code analysis, dependency and secret scanning, and configuration checks. No AI code review ran for this build (no AI key configured, or preview mode); requirements that would need it are shown as "Not verified". Generated code runs with the user's OS privileges under Node's permission model (file system restricted to the project folder); network access is not restricted. No independent human security review was performed unless it is recorded in the human sign-off section below. This is an automated and AI-assisted assessment. It is not a certification and does not replace a professional security review.
limitations: Generated code and its tests run under Node's permission model restricted to the project folder; network access is not restricted.

Some checks were skipped this run: design-freeze (verify-only run (the design on file was used)); scaffold (Your app was not laid out again: this run only checks the code that is already there.); generate (Nothing was written and nothing was spent: this run only checks the code that is already there.); install (node_modules fast path); ai-review (AI is not configured (preview mode)); fix (Nothing was fixed: this run only reports what it found, and fixing is part of a build.).
No independent, professional application-security review of this code has been performed.

topActions.title: Protected route reachable without signing in
topActions.detail: Ensure the route is registered with defineRoute and auth 'user' or 'role:<name>', and that requireAuth is not bypassed.

topActions.title: V8.2.1: Verify that the application ensures that function-level access is restricted to consumers with explicit permissions.
topActions.detail: F-0001: Ensure the route is registered with defineRoute and auth 'user' or 'role:<name>', and that requireAuth is not bypassed.

topActions.title: V8.3.1: Verify that the application enforces authorization rules at a trusted service layer and doesn't rely on controls that an untrusted consumer could manipulate, such as client-side JavaScript.
topActions.detail: F-0001: Ensure the route is registered with defineRoute and auth 'user' or 'role:<name>', and that requireAuth is not bypassed.

topActions.title: V1.2.2: Verify that when dynamically building URLs, untrusted data is encoded according to its context (e.g., URL encoding or base64url encoding for query or path parameters). Ensure that only safe URL protocols are permitted (e.g., disallow javascript: or data:).
topActions.detail: F-0147: Only allow http and https links; otherwise render plain text. F-0149: Only allow http and https links; otherwise render plain text.

topActions.title: V11.2.2: Verify that the application is designed with crypto agility such that random number, authenticated encryption, MAC, or hashing algorithms, key lengths, rounds, ciphers and modes can be reconfigured, upgraded, or swapped at any time, to protect against cryptographic breaks. Similarly, it must also be possible to replace keys and passwords and re-encrypt data. This will allow for seamless upgrades to post-quantum cryptography (PQC), once high-assurance implementations of approved PQC schemes or standards are widely available.
topActions.detail: Add a second key id to FIELD_KEYS, set ACTIVE_FIELD_KEY to it and run npm run rotate-field-key in a test copy. Confirm encrypted values now carry the new key id and still decrypt.
